To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chemotherapeutic drugs, such as dacarbazine, induce intratumoral chemokines that recruit effector T cells to the tumor.

the efficacy of cancer immunotherapies may be enhanced by the use of drugs that induce intratumoral chemokine expression and that this effect is mediated through the activation of a transcription factor called NF-κB.

chemotherapeutic drugs may induce expression of chemokine genes in the tumor and that this expression correlates with T-cell infiltration of the tumor, which may be a key step in the development of novel immunotherapies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel strategies to control T-cell traffic to tumors, with the ultimate goal of improving the efficacy of T cells in the treatment of cancer.
the identification of novel targets and therapeutic approaches to control T-cell homing and function in cancer immunotherapy.
the identification of novel therapeutic strategies aimed at controlling tumor growth and metastases, and at improving the efficacy of T cell-based therapies for cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the next challenge in the immunotherapy of cancer would be to improve T-cell access to tumors.
the use of chemotherapy in the treatment of metastatic melanoma can be associated with a significant improvement in the prognosis of the disease.
chemotherapeutic drugs may have the potential to improve immunotherapy of cancer by inducing the expression of chemokine ligands that attract tumor-specific T cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we showed that chemotherapies induce intratumoral chemokines that can recruit T cells.
we showed that chemokines can play a role in cancer treatment and that we can manipulate the tumor microenvironment to improve the efficacy of immunotherapy.
the tumor microenvironment can be manipulated to enhance immune cell infiltration and to increase the efficacy of immunotherapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

chemotherapeutic drugs may not only kill cancer cells but may also induce the production of chemokines and other factors that promote the infiltration of tumor tissues with T cells and other immune cells.
the efficacy of T cells in the treatment of cancer can be improved by increasing the number of tumor-infiltrating T cells.
the combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy is a promising approach to treat cancer.
